rewrites.5D0C608C: Domestic demand touches the plan at four points. First, the green season. Domestic and visiting-friends trips can fill winter rooms, but school and public holidays recreate peaks, so domestic demand is not counter-seasonal by default. Second, regional spread. A resident's regional break strengthens businesses outside the Metro while moving spend within the province, whereas an interprovincial visitor brings new money. Third, mobility. Domestic visitors without cars need the same shared transport and airport links as international visitors (objective 9). Fourth, inventory. Domestic offers and winter business events draw on the same rooms and experiences, so a night sold should be counted once.
rewrites.45B0F3DE: This study's mandate is international, and domestic channels already exist. Wesgro's With Love from the Locals campaign and Cape Town Tourism's My Cape Town campaign carry regional and local content, and DEDAT's 2026/27 Annual Performance Plan places domestic marketing with the provincial tourism agencies. The plan's target, growth scenarios and indicators are built on international arrivals. Domestic tourism matters to that case as a source of green-season and regional demand, and as a market that rising peak prices could crowd out. The report therefore tracks domestic trips and spend as context (Chapter 5) and leaves a domestic strategy to DEDAT and the provincial tourism agencies.
rewrites.12E2E455: The report tracks international arrivals at Cape Town International as its baseline series and uses the growth model for the cases to 2035. Appendix A2 lists every arrivals figure in circulation and its basis.
rewrites.79DA3FB0: These are complementary lenses, not mutually exclusive industry categories. Air seats are a supply consideration, while air rights and the public decisions that affect them are enabling conditions. Bookability connects distribution with product delivery. Skills support service quality, and local participation affects both the offer and the spread of benefits. A workstream can inform more than one goal.
rewrites.41F716DE: The action plan rests on a central proposition. Coordinated demand, supply and enabling interventions can improve both the visit and the ability of businesses and communities to deliver it. This requires that suitable travellers are reached through effective channels, that the offer is accessible and saleable and that partners sustain the operating conditions. More visits can then be chosen, booked, reached and enjoyed in the intended seasons and places.
rewrites.12A0EE49: Resources and partner commitments support three connected pathways. Demand interventions target suitable travellers, create reasons to travel and convert interest into bookings. Supply interventions improve access, product, service quality and usable capacity. Enabling interventions align decisions, investment, capability, safety, local participation and destination management. Their immediate outputs include saleable offers, distribution arrangements, operational improvements, agreed delivery arrangements and seller training and support.
rewrites.1EA5210B: The proposed mechanism runs as follows. Better-matched offers and fewer barriers to information, booking and travel reduce friction and uncertainty. Visitors are then more able and willing to buy and complete suitable trips, while operators can sell and fulfil them commercially. Where this produces additional visits, longer stays or experience purchases, it can raise visitor value and sustain viable businesses and investment. Geographic and seasonal benefits depend on where and when the additional activity occurs.
rewrites.67A18513: Chapter 3 takes the twenty objectives in turn, each with its challenge or opportunity, evidence, course of action and link to the plan; section 3.4 gives the sequence. Chapter 4 sets out which initiatives run, in what order, with which stakeholders and decision gates. Chapter 5 sets out how progress is measured. Appendices A1 to A9 hold the traceability table, the demand model, the benchmark cases, readiness scores, the community fact base, stakeholder inputs, the action register, the toolkit and references.
rewrites.4DD630AD: The province's share of world travel shows the same gap. Over the three years 2022 to 2024 it took about 0.1% of the world's tourist arrivals and 0.05% of its tourist spend. Its best share of any large air market was the UK's, at 0.27% of air outbound trips. Converting interest is the first task, all year and in every market (section 2.3).[^23]
rewrites.4C9AE1B3: **Long-haul distance and cost.** Every large overseas market is a long-haul flight away, and most visitors must connect to reach the province. The four hub routes through Dubai, Doha, Addis Ababa and Istanbul carried 53% of arrivals on the ten largest routes. No non-stop service links Cape Town to India or China, and a direct Indian route is unlikely before 2030. The Aviation Market Assessment expects carriers to raise fares on full routes before they add seats. In SA Tourism's 2020 brand tracker for the USA, 30% to 50% of respondents at each stage said the country was too expensive to reach, and 27% to 47% said it took too long. This report holds no fare or trip-cost series by market.[^24]
rewrites.441BFCFA: A calendar series confirms the direction. April to September passenger movements at Cape Town International rose from 662,771 in 2015 to 1,342,770 in 2025, international and regional traffic together. That is growth of 102.6%, against 85.7% for the other six months. The green season is a market already won once, which makes further growth credible (section 2.3).
rewrites.376D3A39: The Western Cape's two cases straddle the band. The base case implies 3.8% a year from 2025 to 2035 and the accelerated case 5.3%, and the accelerated case reverts to base unless routes are confirmed. The benchmarking work counts growth as structural only above that band, and only when deliberate changes to demand drivers, access or product drive it, not cyclical recovery or short-term promotion.[^37]
rewrites.27F5F738: Chile was chosen as a long-haul city gateway to coast, wine and wilderness, with Mediterranean seasons like the Western Cape's. South America supplies 55% to 60% of its arrivals. Yet long-haul access was its binding constraint, and Chile treated it as infrastructure. A private concession won in 2015 funded about US$900 million of expansion, under one of the world's most liberal aviation systems built on open-skies agreements. Direct routes now link Santiago with Europe and Australia, and a domestic network carries visitors on to Patagonia and the wine valleys. Santiago's airport traffic rose from about 16 million passengers in 2010 to more than 26 million in 2019. The lesson is blunt: tourism demand follows air access.[^46]
rewrites.57D2C4C1: New Zealand holds coast, wine, nature and culture within short travel distances, as the Western Cape does. Air access economics bind its growth. It moved from awareness-driven marketing to demand generation that answers for specific routes, tying budgets to long-haul corridors and designing campaigns around airline breakeven and shoulder-season loads. Government-backed early-stage route incentives and data shared between tourism bodies and airlines support it. In the regions it curates premium multi-day circuits and limits capacity to protect price. The marketing programme reports more than 16,000 incremental bookings and a return of about NZ$55 million in 2023/24.[^47]
rewrites.7C46C3B5: Singapore was chosen for joining air access, service quality, food culture and visitor segmentation in one approach. Its question was how to turn transit through Changi into stays. Its answer is a stopover programme that the tourism board, Changi Airport Group and Singapore Airlines run under one coordinated strategy. A hotel transformation map and fund lifted quality alongside, moving Singapore from lower-value stopovers towards longer stays and higher spend. Singapore received 16.5 million international visitors in 2024 and record tourism receipts of about S$29 billion.[^48]
rewrites.2E76D391: Melbourne plays the part for Victoria that Cape Town plays for the province: main point of entry, brand anchor and engine of demand. Summer still brings the largest spike in international demand, so Victoria curates a portfolio of events that bring repeat, predictable demand peaks across the year. Melbourne uses its event calendar to lower the risk of new air services and to stimulate aviation demand. Behind the calendar, hotel stock grew 21%, about 5,000 rooms. Melbourne's quietest months still hold 7% of arrivals and its busiest 12%, against 6.1% and 12.7% for the Western Cape on the provisional 2025 shares. The gap is modest, so the lesson is less a flatter curve than an events calendar airlines can plan seats around. Its case rests on stability and yield rather than speed.[^50]
rewrites.649AF281: Air access is infrastructure: Chile funded the expansion of Santiago's airport through a private concession, and New Zealand ties its marketing budgets to long-haul corridors. The Western Cape faces both halves of the access problem Chile and New Zealand attacked: too few seats at the peak and thin demand off it. On the growth model, the base case passes a line of 1.8 million inbound seats by 2030. That line is the model's assumption; in practice the runway binds at peak hours (section 2.4). Off-peak, June carries only 6.4% of the year's international capacity.[^52]
rewrites.0772BDBA: Singapore shows how a hub becomes a destination: its tourism board, airport and airline run one stopover programme under a coordinated strategy. Cape Town's seven largest international routes all connect to global hubs, so the same partnership with the hub carriers is open to it. Government, aviation, events and industry should work to shared KPIs, linking air access, major events and joint marketing. City, provincial and national actors should align around one gateway strategy, with business events treated as a system lever.[^54]
rewrites.4C0F2ED5: The leaders manage quality as a deliberate outcome: Valencia and Singapore set standards through standing bodies rather than leaving them to operators. The results reported for Singapore include longer stays and higher spend per visitor; those for Valencia include more consistent service, a stronger reputation and more repeat visits.[^56]
rewrites.7D848BEC: The cases ask the Western Cape first for a province-wide quality and standards framework led by Wesgro. Within it would sit a provincial quality charter phased by district, with certification visible on booking platforms, alongside standing sector councils for wine, business events, adventure and culture. The cases also ask the province to measure its regions by yield rather than arrivals and to build conservation and community inclusion into the offer.[^57]
rewrites.46E275C2: No single lever explains the leaders' growth: the benchmarking work finds that sustained growth comes from a coordinated destination system in which governance, demand generation and access reinforce one another, not from fragmented interventions. Chile's coordination works best when anchored on a single strategic constraint. The Western Cape's constraint has the same shape as Chile's long-haul access: seats into one gateway airport (section 2.4).[^58]
rewrites.36E56C6A: The evidence also has gaps. No score by criterion is reported, and among the six only New Zealand (3.67) and Kenya (3.50) have a reported score. The margins behind the choice cannot be checked. No case of failure was studied. The nearest local record is the City's own. Its Tourism Development Framework reports uneven past progress and links it to restructuring, thin resources, little support from other departments and weak monitoring. That is a plan, not a destination, so the gap remains. Several comparator charts are unlabelled, so only reported figures are quoted here, and Valencia's figures name no primary source. The route-support recommendation drawn from Chile carries no amount. None of the cases holds Western Cape data, so the province's side of each comparison comes from sections 2.3 to 2.5. The six cases point the same way; the precise rates are indicative.[^68]
